Rest of this afternoon through Friday: The weather over the western 
U.S. will be dominated by a deep upper level low pressure system 
through the res of the work week. The prognoses is for the low to 
become cut off from the Polar Jet, drift slightly further south, and 
sit along the border of California and Nevada for Wednesday and 
Thursday. A slight shift south will allow for the Inland Northwest 
to warm back up wit temperatures rebounding on Wednesday back into 
the 80s. The atmosphere will remain humid with dew point 
temperatures in the 50s for the Idaho Panhandle into extreme 
eastern Washington. Surface based CAPE values will increase to 
between 500-1000 J/kg, but there will also be a considerable 
amount of convective inhibition (CIN) that will cap convection. 
A shortwave disturbance rounding the upper level low will spark 
off convection across southern to central Idaho and this 
convection may push far enough north to get into the Camas 
Prairie into the Central Panhandle Mountains around late 
afternoon. Outflow boundaries from nearby thunderstorms may also
spark off new convective cells and this could result in a 
further northwestward extent of thunderstorms into the Lewiston-
Clarkston Valley, Pullman/Moscow, and St. Maries. Confidence in 
this scenario occurring is low, but people planning to enjoy 
outdoor activities late in the day for these areas should keep 
their eyes open and be prepared for this potential.

Temperatures increase further on Thursday up 5-10 degrees compared 
to Wednesday. Widespread upper 80s to low 90s is expected and 
this will bring minor to moderate HeatRisk. Dew points increase 
a bit more as well into the upper 50s to near 60 in the Idaho 
Panhandle into extreme eastern Washington and into the mid 50s 
into the Cascades as well. Thursday will be the warmest and 
muggiest day of the week, and it will set the table for 
thunderstorms later in the day. The big question is how much 
forcing will we see synoptically to kick off convection. Surface
based CAPE values Thursday increase to 1000-2000 J/kg overall, 
and may be even higher over the southeast with highs in the 
upper 80s and dew points near 60; but, we will also have CIN of 
40-80 J/kg. Deterministic guidance does show a bit more of a 
robust shortwave round the upper low for Thursday evening, and 
there is moderate confidence that this will be enough to get 
convection going. All areas will see at least a 15% chance for 
thunderstorms, and those chances increase to around 30% over the
southeast portion of the forecast area. Mid level lapse rates 
will be quite steep even through the night on Thursday, and I 
expect that we will see convection continuing through the night.
Evening convection on Thursday with such high CAPE values will 
be strong to potentially severe. Large hail will be a potential 
threat along with the potential for strong to damaging wind 
gusts. P-wats up over an inch will also result in torrential 
downpours and this could lead to flash flooding for areas, 
especially those in steep terrain, near burn scars, or 
urbanized areas.

A shortwave push across the eastern Pacific on Friday will kick
out the upper level low and also kick off additional convection
for Friday afternoon. Main threat area for strong to isolated 
severe thunderstorms will be over the northern half of the 
forecast area and over the Idaho Panhandle. Better steering flow
on Friday will result in more movement in the storms, which 
will help decrease the flash flood threat a little bit; but, 
storms will continue to tap into a juicy atmosphere and likely 
be just as wet as Thursday. The westerly gradient will also 
tight across the region on Friday and this will result in gusty 
winds through the Cascades for the afternoon and evening. There
is a 40-50% chance for wind gusts up to 40-45 mph for the 
Wenatchee Area, Waterville Plateau, and the western Columbia 
Basin.

Friday night through Monday: The disturbance that moves across 
on Friday looks to push much of the moisture and instability 
east of the region by Saturday. It also will bring temperatures 
down a bit with temperatures back down to near normal in the 60s
to low 70s. Overall a much drier forecast for the weekend and 
occasionally breezy. Showers and isolated thunderstorms may hang
on over the Idaho Panhandle on Saturday depending on how 
quickly the shortwave moves through and then more confident for 
drier conditions Sunday into Monday. /SVH
